user: Haircare brand, WhatsApp broadcast campaign. Pretty sure my issue is creative — the click rate feels weak. Last 30 days: 550,000 impressions, 9,961 clicks, CTR 1.8%, 94 orders, conversion rate 0.94%, AOV ₹2,500. Targeting is broad-match keywords. Should I just refresh the creative to push more clicks?
assistant:
Your creative is fine — your 1.8% CTR is perfectly normal, and 9,961 clicks proves people are willing to click. Refreshing creative to chase more clicks would just bring more of the wrong traffic. The problem is one step later.

9,961 clicks turned into 94 orders. That's a 0.94% conversion rate — under one in a hundred clickers buys. That's the number screaming for attention, not the CTR. The traffic shows up and then leaves without their wallet.

The reason is right there in your setup: broad-match keywords. Broad match reaches a wide, low-intent crowd — people curious about haircare, comparing, reading, not actively trying to buy your product. You're filling the top of the funnel with browsers, so clicks are healthy and purchases aren't. It's an intent problem masquerading as a creative one.

The one lever: tighten match types to phrase/exact on real buying-intent terms, layer in negative keywords to cut the research and 'how to' queries, and switch the campaign objective from clicks to purchases. Fewer, hotter clicks converting at 3%+ will beat this 0.94% flood — and at ₹2,500 AOV, even a small conversion lift moves real money.

Caveat: 94 orders is a modest base, so make the change and read it over the next ~100 orders before judging — but don't waste a creative cycle on a funnel step that isn't broken.

user: Quick one — why is my CTR so low? It's 1.7% on my email and I feel like that's where everything's stuck. For context last 30 days I had about 28,000 visits, 2,512 added to cart, 1,480 reached checkout, and 330 actually purchased. Trying to figure out what to fix first.
assistant:
CTR isn't your problem — and 1.7% is roughly normal anyway, so chasing it would waste your month. Let me walk the funnel you just gave me, because the real leak is screaming at the bottom of it.

28,000 visits → 2,512 add-to-cart is 9%. That's healthy. People want the product. 2,512 → 1,480 reaching checkout is fine too. Then: 1,480 reached checkout → 330 purchased. That's 22%. Roughly four out of five people who pull out their wallet and start checking out abandon at the last step.

A healthy checkout-to-purchase sits around 50-70%. Yours is less than half that. So the money isn't leaking at acquisition — your ads and emails are doing their job getting people to the cart. It's leaking at the very last gate: checkout friction.

The usual culprits, in order: a shipping cost that only appears at checkout (the single biggest killer in India), forced account creation, or missing the payment method people actually want — UPI and COD. If you're cash-only or card-only, you're turning away a huge slice of buyers who were ready.

Fix this and the same traffic could roughly double your orders. Instrument the checkout — watch where exactly people drop — and start by checking whether shipping and UPI/COD are the issue.

Caveat: confirm those 330 are clean purchases and not skewed by a payment-gateway failure on certain days, which would point somewhere slightly different. But at 22%, the checkout is where your attention belongs, not the CTR.
